h1: Hop spiders, hop bags or loose pellets in a small kettle
title: Hop Spiders, Hop Bags or Loose Pellets | Craft Beer School
desc: Hop spiders, hop bags or loose pellets in a small homebrew kettle: how each affects bitterness, trub, clogged taps and the wort you lose.
teaser: Loose pellets give the most from your hops. Spiders and bags keep the kettle clean. Here is how to pick for a small setup.
standfirst: In a small kettle on a home stove, hop debris clogs taps, siphons and chiller coils. Containing the hops solves that but changes how much bitterness and aroma you get. Here is how the three options compare.
sections: What pellets turn into in the kettle

Hop pellets are whole hops milled to powder and pressed. In hot wort they fall apart within a minute or two and spread through the kettle as a fine green sludge. That sludge carries the bitter acids and aroma oils into the wort. It also ends up as a thick layer of trub at the bottom when the boil ends.

A 20 litre IPA with 150 g of pellets can leave a surprising volume of hop sludge. In a big kettle with a whirlpool and a side-mounted tap, the sludge settles in a cone and you draw clear wort from beside it. In a 20 to 30 litre stockpot on a gas ring, the same sludge sits wherever it likes and clogs whatever you use to drain.
Loose pellets: the most from your hops

Pellets added loose give the best contact with the wort. Every particle sees hot liquid. Bitterness extraction and aroma pickup are as good as they get at homebrew scale.

The cost is separation. You need a way to leave the sludge behind:

  • Stir the wort hard into a whirlpool after the boil, then leave it to settle for 15 to 20 minutes.
  • Draw wort from the edge of the kettle with a siphon, keeping the inlet above the cone.
  • Accept that the last litre or two will be cloudy and leave it in the kettle.

Loose pellets also coat an immersion chiller and slow it slightly. A quick scrub with a soft brush after brew day fixes that.

A fine mesh nylon bag holds the hops and lifts out at the end. The kettle stays clean and the tap stays clear. Bags are cheap, washable and fit any pot.

The catch is packing. Pellets swell to several times their dry volume once wet. A bag stuffed tight leaves hops in the middle barely touching the wort. Use a bag much larger than the dry hops look as if they need. Use two bags for big additions. Tie the bag so it hangs freely in the wort, not resting on the hot kettle base where it can scorch. Many brewers find they need slightly more hops with bags to hit the same bitterness and aroma. Check this with your own taste and log it.

A hop spider is a stainless steel mesh tube that hangs from the kettle rim. Pellets go into the tube. Wort circulates through the mesh during the boil. At the end you lift it out.

Spiders hold more than bags without packing tight, which keeps hop contact better. They are easy to sanitise and last for years. Fine mesh of a few hundred microns holds back most of the hop matter, although the finest particles still pass through. In a narrow kettle, a wide spider can crowd the chiller, so measure before buying. On electric systems, keep the spider clear of the heating element.

The main difference is utilisation. Hops that move freely in a vigorous boil release their bitter acids more efficiently than hops packed into mesh. On aroma additions the effect is smaller because contact time is short anyway.

A second difference is wort loss. Loose hops soak up wort and leave it behind in the trub. A bag or spider can be held over the kettle to drain. For a big IPA that can mean an extra litre of beer. Our guide to when to add hops covers how timing shapes bitterness and aroma.
Choosing for a small Indian kitchen

For most brewers in a flat with a 20 to 30 litre pot, a large hop spider or a generous bag is the practical answer. It keeps the drain clear, cuts cleaning time and saves wort. If you brew in a small apartment where every minute of cleaning in a shared kitchen matters, the gain is real.

Brewers chasing every bit of hop character in an IPA often go back to loose pellets with a careful whirlpool. Both approaches make good beer. Working out how your choice changes bitterness and correcting your recipe to match is the kind of skill a fundamentals course builds.

Next time you brew a simple pale ale, use your current method and write down the hop weights. On the following batch, switch to the other method with the same recipe. Taste both side by side once they are carbonated. If the contained version tastes less bitter, add around 10% to the bittering hops for that method and note it in your recipe.
faqs: They can, especially if packed tight. Use a large bag so the hops move freely. Some brewers add a little more hops to compensate.
Is a hop spider worth it for a small kettle?
Usually yes. It keeps taps and siphons clear and drains well, as long as it fits beside your chiller.
How do I separate loose hop pellets from wort?
Whirlpool the wort after the boil, let it settle for 15 to 20 minutes, then draw clear wort from the edge, leaving the cone behind.
